paragraphs: This paper studies how to reduce the step size in stochastic gradient descent when optimizing a convex objective. The step size controls how far each update moves. Rather than treating its schedule as a separate tuning choice, the authors connect the schedule to a property of the objective that they formally define as curvature.

The main contribution is a framework for characterizing that curvature and deriving an inequality from it. This inequality makes it possible to compute an optimal sequence of diminishing step sizes by solving a differential equation. The approach therefore connects the shape of the optimization problem, the choice of updates, and the expected rate of progress within one theoretical analysis.

The exact solutions recover results already known in the literature, while also allowing the authors to characterize a new regularizer and its expected convergence rates. These findings concern convex objectives and diminishing step sizes; they explain how the proposed curvature framework organizes convergence behavior in that setting.
icml-2019-characterization-of-convex-obj.tldr: A formal notion of convex-objective curvature connects diminishing SGD step sizes to optimal expected convergence rates.

paragraphs: An agent that learns over its lifetime should be able to reuse existing skills when a new task appears. This paper asks how to combine those skills in a principled way. Its focus is value functions, which express the value of behavior in a task and provide a basis for composing previously learned capabilities.

Under the assumption of deterministic dynamics, the authors prove that optimal value functions can be composed in entropy-regularized reinforcement learning. They also extend the result to standard reinforcement learning. The deterministic-dynamics assumption is part of the theoretical claim: the abstract does not establish the same result for environments whose transitions are inherently random.

The authors demonstrate composition in a high-dimensional video game. An agent equipped with a library of skills solves new tasks immediately, without further learning. This connects the mathematical result to a concrete example of skill reuse: learning the component skills in advance can enable new behavior through composition when the task and environment support it.
icml-2019-composing-value-functions-in-r.tldr: Under deterministic dynamics, composing optimal value functions enables principled skill reuse, demonstrated on new video-game tasks without further learning.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic text model that keeps word identity and word order in its input representation. It represents each document as a sequence of high-dimensional one-hot vectors, rather than discarding order or first compressing words into dense vectors. Convolutional Poisson factor analysis, or CPFA, operates directly on this sequence.

CPFA groups words into phrases and discovers specific topics at the phrase level. The authors extend it into a convolutional Poisson gamma belief network by connecting CPFA to a gamma belief network through a new probabilistic pooling layer. This produces a hierarchy in which more specific phrase topics feed into increasingly general topics.

The paper develops two inference approaches: a Gibbs sampler and a convolutional variational autoencoder based on Weibull distributions. Experiments show that the resulting model learns high-quality latent text representations that capture word order. The stated broader opportunity is to use this component to enrich existing latent-variable models that otherwise ignore order, bringing phrase structure into their representations.
icml-2019-convolutional-poisson-gamma-be.tldr: A convolutional probabilistic text model preserves word order while learning a hierarchy of phrase-level topics.

paragraphs: Forecasting many related time series requires learning shared patterns while also describing uncertainty. This paper combines two approaches with complementary strengths. Classical models use strong structural assumptions to work efficiently with limited data and estimate uncertainty, while deep neural networks can learn complex patterns and dependencies when sufficient data are available.

The proposed hybrid assigns shared structure to a latent global component built with deep learning. A local classical model handles uncertainty. This division gives the method a way to learn across a large collection of series while retaining a local modeling component, rather than asking a single type of model to provide every capability.

The theoretical analysis supplies a necessary and sufficient decomposition of exchangeable time series into global and local parts. That exchangeability setting is central to the stated decomposition. Experiments additionally show advantages in data efficiency and computational complexity. Together, the theory and experiments support the proposed combination as a scalable approach to probabilistic forecasting for collections of related series.
icml-2019-deep-factors-for-forecasting-a.tldr: Deep Factors combines a global deep model with local classical models to forecast related time series and represent uncertainty.

paragraphs: This paper studies private learning with smooth, non-convex losses. Earlier approaches often measured solution quality using gradient norms, but a small gradient does not generally guarantee a good objective value. The authors instead analyze expected excess empirical or population risk, bringing a more direct measure of loss quality into this privacy setting.

They establish an upper bound with dependence on dimension, privacy parameters, and the logarithm of the sample size. For empirical risk, a more detailed analysis of time-averaged error improves the inverse-logarithmic sample dependence to an inverse-polynomial dependence when dimension is constant. This qualification matters because the stronger sample-size result is stated specifically for that dimensional setting.

The paper also studies more efficient algorithms through the connection between privacy and approximate local optimization. With sufficiently many samples, private algorithms can find approximate local minima with high probability, in both constrained and unconstrained problems. These results show that escaping saddle points is compatible with differential privacy under the stated conditions, alongside the separate guarantees on excess risk.
icml-2019-differentially-private-empiric.tldr: The paper bounds excess risk for private non-convex learning and shows that private algorithms can reach approximate local minima with sufficient data.

paragraphs: EigenDamage aims to reduce the resources a neural network needs during inference while retaining its accuracy. It addresses structured pruning: removing parts of a network using information about how those removals affect the objective. The central change is to represent the network in different coordinates before deciding what to prune.

The authors introduce a reparameterization based on the Kronecker-factored eigenbasis and apply Hessian-based pruning within that representation. In this basis, different weights are approximately independent. That approximate separation supports more accurate pruning decisions and fast computation, compared with applying Hessian-based pruning directly in the original parameter coordinates.

Experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness, with particularly significant improvements on more challenging datasets and networks. An iterative version reduces wide ResNet32's model size by a factor of ten and its floating-point operation count by a factor of eight, with negligible accuracy loss. These reported reductions illustrate how changing the representation used for pruning can materially improve the trade-off between inference resources and predictive performance.
icml-2019-eigendamage-structured-pruning.tldr: EigenDamage prunes networks in a basis where weights are approximately independent, enabling substantial compression with little reported accuracy loss.

paragraphs: This paper considers a practical situation: a black-box predictor has been chosen because it performs better than interpretable alternatives. The authors seek transparency on a subset of inputs where a simpler model is already accurate enough. The remaining inputs continue to use the black-box predictor, making interpretability a property of part of the system's decisions.

Their Hybrid Rule Sets model uses decision rules to identify and handle regions where those rules match or nearly match the supplied black box's accuracy. Training uses an iterative search algorithm, with theoretically grounded strategies for reducing computation. The framework is agnostic to the black box during training, making the partial-substitution idea applicable without tying it to a particular black-box architecture.

Experiments on structured and text data support the usefulness of this hybrid approach. The intended benefit is an interpretable portion of predictions with little or no predictive-performance cost. The scope of transparency is therefore tied to the subset covered by the rules, while the black box remains responsible for the rest.
icml-2019-gaining-free-or-low-cost-inter.tldr: Hybrid Rule Sets substitute understandable rules for a black box on selected inputs while aiming to preserve predictive performance.

paragraphs: This paper introduces graph convolutional Gaussian processes for observations that are functions defined on graphs. The goal is to learn translation-invariant relationships on domains that need not have the ordinary geometry of a flat grid. This extends the modeling idea of convolution to inputs whose underlying structure is a general graph.

The proposed method is Bayesian and nonparametric. Its model structure is designed to accommodate high-dimensional inputs while retaining expressive power, a motivation shared with convolutional neural networks. The graph supplies the domain on which each observation is defined, allowing the same broad framework to address different kinds of structured input.

The authors apply the method to images and triangular meshes. These applications demonstrate versatility across the two domains, and the reported comparisons are favorable to existing methods despite the models' relative simplicity. The contribution is therefore both a model construction and evidence of its usefulness: convolutional structure can be incorporated into Gaussian processes for learning relationships on graph-based domains.
icml-2019-graph-convolutional-gaussian-p.tldr: Graph convolutional Gaussian processes bring expressive Bayesian modeling to high-dimensional observations defined on graphs.

paragraphs: This paper tackles overfitting in large neural language models by introducing adversarial noise during training. The noise is applied to the output embedding layer, making the regularizer act on a specific part of the model. The aim is to improve generalization by training the model against deliberately challenging perturbations.

The authors show that the optimal adversarial noise has a closed-form solution. This makes the resulting algorithm simple and time efficient. Their theoretical analysis connects the mechanism to greater diversity among embedding vectors, which helps explain how the perturbations can increase model robustness rather than merely adding arbitrary disturbance to training.

On Penn Treebank and Wikitext-2, the method improves the reported single-model state of the art, with test perplexities of 46.01 and 38.65 respectively. The authors also apply it to machine translation, reporting higher BLEU scores than several transformer-based baselines on WMT14 English-German and IWSLT14 German-English. These findings provide evidence that the same training mechanism can help both language modeling and translation.
icml-2019-improving-neural-language-mode.tldr: Closed-form adversarial noise at the output embedding layer regularizes language models and improves reported language-modeling and translation results.

paragraphs: gradKCCA seeks nonlinear relationships between paired data representations using kernel functions. Standard kernel canonical correlation analysis relies on a kernel matrix, which can become a scaling bottleneck. This paper changes the optimization problem so that it can discover kernel-based relationships without constructing or relying on that matrix.

The key constraint is that projection directions in the kernel-induced feature space must have corresponding preimages in the original data space. This lets the authors optimize with alternating projected-gradient updates directly in that original space. They also constrain the preimages' L1 norms to control sparsity, making the discovered patterns easier to interpret.

This formulation links computational efficiency and interpretability through the same choice of representation. The preimage requirement enables optimization outside the kernel matrix, while sparsity control makes the projection patterns more selective. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets report better speed and noise robustness than state-of-the-art CCA methods. These are empirical findings for the evaluated datasets, supporting the usefulness of the modified formulation.
icml-2019-large-scale-sparse-kernel-cano.tldr: gradKCCA avoids the kernel-matrix bottleneck and adds sparsity control, with reported gains in speed and noise robustness.

paragraphs: Weak supervision combines labels from multiple noisy sources without requiring ground-truth labels to estimate their accuracies. A major challenge is that those sources may depend on one another. This paper studies how to learn that dependency structure, so the combined model can account for relationships among its sources.

The authors analyze an algorithm based on robust principal component analysis and establish improved recovery rates. Under certain conditions, the required amount of unlabeled data grows sublinearly, or even logarithmically, with the number of sources. These results exploit the sparsity pattern of dependencies, improving on earlier analyses with linear scaling. An information-theoretic lower bound also characterizes the minimum sample requirements of the weak-supervision setting.

On real-world relation extraction and image classification tasks, the method improves over approaches assuming conditionally independent sources by up to 4.64 F1 points. It improves over previous structure-learning approaches by up to 4.41 points. Together, the theoretical and empirical results show why modeling source dependencies can improve both data requirements and predictive performance.
icml-2019-learning-dependency-structures.tldr: Learning sparse dependencies among noisy labeling sources can reduce unlabeled-data requirements under stated conditions and improve weak-supervision accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose items when their eventual display order is fixed by an explicit rule. Selecting a good set is different from simply finding individually strong items, because the final ordered list is the object being evaluated. The predefined order may have little relationship to item quality.

A motivating example is a personalized feed that displays items by publication time. The system can choose which items appear, but the display rule determines their positions. The authors formulate this as a learning problem and propose theoretically grounded algorithms that directly optimize the quality of the list produced after the ordering rule is applied.

Offline and online experiments with a large-scale product search engine report substantial advantages over the baselines across all key quality metrics evaluated. The findings support treating selection and its resulting order together. For systems with a fixed ordering convention, the relevant optimization target is the quality of the displayed sequence, rather than a ranking the interface will never actually use.
icml-2019-learning-to-select-for-a-prede.tldr: The paper learns which items to select by optimizing list quality under a predefined display order.

paragraphs: Manifold Mixup addresses neural networks that make confident mistakes on inputs differing from their training examples. It adds a training signal by interpolating hidden representations and encouraging less confident predictions on those interpolations. The regularizer therefore acts inside the network, shaping how it behaves between learned representations.

The authors connect this training procedure to smoother decision boundaries at multiple representation levels. They also find flatter class representations, meaning that examples within a class vary along fewer directions. The paper proves why such flattening occurs under ideal conditions, checks it empirically in practical settings, and relates the result to information theory and generalization.

The reported benefits include improvements over strong supervised-learning baselines, better robustness to single-step adversarial attacks, and improved test log-likelihood. The method requires only a few lines of code and adds no significant computation according to the abstract. Its findings connect a lightweight training change to both representation geometry and measured predictive behavior, with the theoretical explanation explicitly depending on ideal conditions.
icml-2019-manifold-mixup-better-represen.tldr: Manifold Mixup trains on interpolated hidden states to smooth decisions and flatten class representations, improving several reported generalization measures.

paragraphs: This paper estimates the distribution of success probabilities across a population when each individual has only a few observations. Each of N independent individuals has a probability drawn from an unknown distribution, and contributes t independent Bernoulli trials. The target is the population distribution, particularly when t is much smaller than N.

The authors prove that maximum likelihood estimation is efficiently computable and minimax optimal in this sparse setting. For sufficiently large N and t below c log N, it achieves an earth mover's distance error of order 1/t. Over an exponentially large interval of t beyond that threshold, it achieves order 1/sqrt(t log N).

The comparison is with a naive plug-in estimator, whose error remains of order 1/sqrt(t) regardless of population size. Thus, estimating the distribution through maximum likelihood can use a large population more effectively than simply collecting individual estimates into a distribution. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also demonstrate good performance, complementing the stated optimality guarantees.
icml-2019-maximum-likelihood-estimation-.tldr: Maximum likelihood efficiently achieves optimal distribution-estimation rates when many individuals each provide few Bernoulli observations.

paragraphs: This paper measures semantic similarity by comparing probabilistic explanations of two groups of embeddings. For sentences, the central question is whether a model that treats the two sentences jointly explains their word embeddings better than a model that does not. Similarity becomes a model-comparison problem rather than only a direct comparison of vectors.

The framework makes explicit assumptions about how word embeddings are generated. It uses information criteria to compare models while still penalizing complexity, addressing some shortcomings of Bayesian model comparison. This penalty matters because the comparison should weigh explanatory fit together with the complexity of the explanation.

Applied to Semantic Textual Similarity datasets, the framework produces competitive results when paired with an appropriate likelihood. The likelihood choice is therefore part of the stated empirical finding. The contribution is a probabilistic way to reason about semantic grouping: whether two collections belong together depends on how well joint modeling accounts for their embeddings relative to the alternative, with complexity included in the assessment.
icml-2019-model-comparison-for-semantic-.tldr: Semantic similarity is estimated by comparing joint and separate probabilistic explanations of embedding groups while penalizing model complexity.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to encourage diversity when learning non-convex models, especially mixture models. If mixture components collapse into similar solutions, the model may fail to capture different patterns in the data. Encouraging the components to differ is presented as a way to counter that collapse and support more robust learning.

The authors formulate diversity-promoting learning as a variational optimization problem. They use an entropy functional as the mechanism for encouraging diversity and develop a simple, efficient algorithm based on functional gradients. The resulting method significantly generalizes Stein variational gradient descent, placing diversity within the optimization objective itself.

Experiments cover challenging real-world problems, including deep embedded clustering and deep anomaly detection. The reported results show substantial improvements over existing methods and support the effectiveness of the diversity mechanism. The contribution connects an explicit mathematical objective for diversity with an algorithm for optimizing it, providing evidence that this approach can help models represent a wider range of patterns in the evaluated applications.
icml-2019-nonlinear-stein-variational-gr.tldr: An entropy-based variational objective generalizes SVGD to encourage diverse mixture components and improve reported clustering and anomaly-detection results.

paragraphs: Adversarial training alternates between finding inputs that increase classification loss and updating the network to reduce loss on those inputs. This paper examines the quality of the inner search. It asks how well the attack optimization has converged, and how that quality should change over the course of training.

The authors introduce the First-Order Stationary Condition for constrained optimization as a quantitative measure of convergence quality. Using this criterion, they find that better-converged adversarial examples are essential for better robustness later in training. Early in training, however, high convergence quality is unnecessary and may even harm the resulting robustness.

These observations motivate a dynamic strategy that gradually raises the convergence quality of generated adversarial examples. The paper reports significant robustness improvements and supports the method with theoretical and empirical results. Its practical implication is that the inner optimization deserves a training schedule of its own: the quality of adversarial examples should be considered together with the stage at which they are used.
icml-2019-on-the-convergence-and-robustn.tldr: Gradually increasing adversarial-example convergence quality improves robustness, reflecting different needs early and late in training.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how well a target policy would perform using observations gathered under another policy. This paper focuses on improving an existing estimator for that task. Given a base estimator and a parameterized family of control variates, the authors seek a choice that reduces the estimator's risk.

Their analysis expresses population risk as a function of the control-variate parameters. This makes the relationship between the chosen correction and estimation quality explicit. They also establish conditions that guarantee an improvement in risk, so the theoretical contribution identifies when selecting a control variate is beneficial rather than treating improvement as automatic.

The main results concern multi-armed bandits. The authors additionally propose a simple design for contextual bandits and evaluate the resulting estimator on multiclass cost-sensitive classification datasets, where it performs well. The work combines an analytical approach to estimator design with a contextual application, showing how a specified family of corrections can be studied and used to improve off-policy evaluation.
icml-2019-on-the-design-of-estimators-fo.tldr: The paper derives how control-variate choices affect off-policy estimation risk and establishes conditions for improving a base estimator.

paragraphs: A common way to process a set is to map its elements into a latent space and sum their representations. Summation makes the result independent of element order. This paper investigates whether the latent dimension can stay fixed as the maximum number of elements in the input sets increases.

The authors show that an earlier argument supporting fixed dimensionality depends on highly discontinuous mappings. They argue that those mappings have limited practical use. They then analyze continuous mappings, including those supplied by neural networks or Gaussian processes, and prove that continuity imposes a lower bound on the latent dimension.

For universal function representation within this continuous sum-based model, the latent dimension must be at least as large as the maximum input-set size. The result is about the capacity to represent functions universally, rather than a claim that every individual task requires that dimension. It identifies a concrete architectural constraint: permutation invariance through summation does not remove the representational demands created by larger sets.
icml-2019-on-the-limitations-of-represen.tldr: Continuous sum-based set models need latent dimension at least equal to maximum set size for universal function representation.

paragraphs: This paper develops visual question-answering models in which symbolic programs are latent stochastic variables. The program represents a reasoning procedure, while the probabilistic formulation allows uncertainty over which program applies. This gives the model an explicit reasoning structure that can be examined alongside its predicted answer.

The authors identify two advantages over prior neural-symbolic approaches. The generated programs are more understandable while requiring fewer teaching examples, and the model supports counterfactual questions about which programs could produce a specified answer for a given image. Such queries allow inspection of the model's beliefs about possible reasoning paths, extending interpretation beyond reading a single predicted program.

Results on CLEVR and SHAPES support these claims. The model improves program and answer prediction accuracy even when data are limited, and its probabilistic structure allows the coherence and consistency of reasoning to be probed. The contribution therefore combines predictive learning with a way to investigate how alternative symbolic explanations relate to the image and the proposed answer.
icml-2019-probabilistic-neural-symbolic-.tldr: Probabilistic symbolic programs improve reported visual question-answering accuracy and enable counterfactual inspection of reasoning.

paragraphs: This paper studies imitation learning from a finite collection of expert trajectories when no reinforcement signal is available. One traditional route first recovers an expert reward function and then performs reinforcement learning, which can be indirect and expensive. Adversarial approaches that match expert and agent policy distributions can instead face training instability.

The proposed framework estimates the support of the expert policy: the region of behavior represented by that policy. It uses this estimate to construct a fixed reward function. Once that reward is available, the imitation problem can be handled within a standard reinforcement-learning setup, giving the learning agent a stable reward definition to optimize.

Experiments in discrete and continuous domains demonstrate the usefulness of the reward function under different reinforcement-learning algorithms. Reported performance is comparable to or better than the state of the art. The central contribution is the conversion from demonstrations to a fixed training signal through support estimation, with the experiments showing that this signal can support effective imitation across the evaluated settings.
icml-2019-random-expert-distillation-imi.tldr: Estimating expert-policy support turns demonstrations into a fixed reward for standard reinforcement learning, with competitive reported imitation performance.

paragraphs: This paper addresses performance disparities across groups defined by sensitive attributes while keeping an existing classifier fixed. It begins from the observation that group disparities can be described through input and output distributions. The proposed intervention changes the input distribution for the disadvantaged group, with the aim of closing the performance gap.

The authors call the modified input distribution a counterfactual distribution and characterize its properties for common fairness criteria. They introduce a descent algorithm to learn such a distribution from data. The estimated distribution can then guide construction of a data preprocessor, allowing intervention before inputs reach the black-box classifier.

Experiments on real-world datasets show that this approach can repair different forms of disparity without a significant decrease in accuracy. The method's objective is to eliminate the gap, while the empirical finding establishes successful reductions in the evaluated settings. Its contribution is a distribution-based route to modifying a deployed classifier's group-level outcomes without training a replacement model.
icml-2019-repairing-without-retraining-a.tldr: Learned changes to disadvantaged-group input distributions can reduce a fixed classifier's disparities through preprocessing without retraining.

paragraphs: SATNet integrates a logical optimization component into a larger neural learning system. Its central ingredient is a differentiable, smoothed maximum satisfiability solver. Making this component differentiable allows training signals to pass through the reasoning step, so the surrounding system can be learned end to end.

The approximate solver uses fast coordinate descent on a semidefinite program associated with the satisfiability problem. The authors derive how to differentiate through its solution analytically and compute the backward pass efficiently. This provides a concrete mechanism for combining a structured logical computation with neural-network training.

The demonstrations include learning parity with single-bit supervision and learning to solve 9-by-9 Sudoku from examples. A visual Sudoku system combines the solver with a convolutional architecture to map puzzle images to logical solutions. These results show that the integrated approach can learn challenging logical structure with limited forms of supervision. They support the promise of differentiable reasoning components while retaining the paper's characterization of the solver as approximate.
icml-2019-satnet-bridging-deep-learning-.tldr: SATNet makes an approximate satisfiability solver differentiable, enabling end-to-end systems that learn tasks including parity and visual Sudoku.

paragraphs: This paper targets two difficulties with recurrent neural networks: understanding what they have learned and handling sequences that require long-term memory. The authors introduce state regularization, a stochastic transition mechanism placed between recurrent cell applications. It makes the network transition among a finite collection of learnable states.

The approach is evaluated on regular languages, where extracting an automaton provides a way to inspect learned behavior. It is also evaluated on nonregular languages and tasks requiring external memory, including balanced parentheses, palindromes, and copying. Additional experiments cover sentiment analysis, visual object recognition, and language modeling.

The reported findings show that state regularization simplifies extracting finite-state automata from recurrent transition dynamics and makes the networks more interpretable. It also encourages operation resembling an automaton with external memory rather than a finite-state machine alone. This distinction connects the two motivations: a more understandable transition structure can coexist with behavior that relies on memory beyond the finite collection of control states.
icml-2019-state-regularized-recurrent-ne.tldr: Stochastic transitions among learnable states make recurrent networks easier to interpret and encourage behavior resembling automata with external memory.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what Gaussian weight priors imply for the internal units of deep Bayesian neural networks. Such priors are commonly associated with L2 weight regularization, but the authors examine a different level of the model: the distributions induced on unit values before and after activation.

For the studied networks, which use a class of ReLU-like nonlinearities, the main result is that these induced distributions become increasingly heavy-tailed with depth. The analysis identifies Gaussian behavior in the first layer, sub-exponential behavior in the second, and sub-Weibull distributions in deeper layers. These distribution classes describe how the tails change as the network grows deeper.

The result reveals a more intricate regularization effect than the weight-decay interpretation alone conveys. Specifying Gaussian weights does not make the induced behavior of deep units equally Gaussian throughout the network. Simulation experiments corroborate the theoretical analysis, supporting the connection between layer depth and the changing unit-level distributions under the stated prior and nonlinearity assumptions.
icml-2019-understanding-priors-in-bayesi.tldr: Gaussian weight priors induce increasingly heavy-tailed unit distributions with depth in the studied Bayesian networks.
